note.question: When do commercial repricing algorithms intensify price competition, and when can simple undercut-and-reset rules sustain tacitly collusive price cycles?
note.overview: Merchants strategically delegate pricing to fixed-price, undercutting, or undercut-and-reset algorithms. The paper derives Nash equilibria in delegated strategy parameters, a mixed Nash equilibrium in technology choice, and KMR-style evolutionary steady states, then matches the implied price cycles to e-commerce data.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Merchants choose an available pricing technology and commit to it, then choose its parameters in Nash fashion. Once paired, the algorithms alternately quote prices as mechanical functions of the rival's previous price. In the evolutionary layer, merchants are randomly matched and one merchant per period may myopically switch technology in response to current population shares, subject to inertia and rare mistakes. Delegation restricts merchants to a small rule set and yields sharper predictions than an unrestricted repeated-pricing folk theorem.

components.label: Equilibrium or solution concept
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Nash equilibrium in delegated pricing strategies with a mixed technology-choice equilibrium and KMR steady states. Proposition 1 gives the U-versus-C continuum of parameter equilibria; Proposition 4 shows the cycle average equals monopoly price under symmetry; the technology-choice payoff matrix yields a unique symmetric mixed Nash equilibrium; Propositions 5-6 and Corollary 1 characterize evolutionary steady states and transition prices.
